title: From Mayfair to the Frozen Aisle: A Two-Michelin Indian Kitchen Bets on America's Pantry
excerpt: Gymkhana Fine Foods lands exclusively in Whole Foods nationwide on the back of an $8.5 million raise, wagering that NRIs and curious Americans will pay a premium for restaurant-grade curry at home.
body:
For decades, the at-home Indian meal in America meant one of two extremes: hours at the stove grinding masalas, or a jar of gloopy supermarket "curry sauce" that bore little resemblance to anything served in a good restaurant. Gymkhana, the two-Michelin-starred London dining room, is betting that a generation of busy NRIs and adventurous American cooks will pay to close that gap — and it has chosen Whole Foods as the place to make its case.

Gymkhana Fine Foods, the consumer-packaged-goods arm born from the celebrated Mayfair restaurant, has launched nationwide and exclusively at Whole Foods Market stores and online. The debut is backed by an $8.5 million Series A funding round (roughly £6.3 million) led by CAVU Consumer Partners, the firm co-founded by "Shark Tank" investor Rohan Oza, whose past bets include Poppi and Beyond Meat. CAVU had already led the brand's 2024 seed round, and Oza along with managing partner Jared Jacobs sit on the company's board.

## Context & Background

The brand sits inside JKS Restaurants, the London empire founded by siblings Jyotin, Karam and Sunaina Sethi. JKS operates more than 30 Indian concepts — among them Trishna, Brigadiers, BiBi and the New York Punjabi room Ambassadors Clubhouse — and counts eight Michelin stars and six Bib Gourmand mentions across the group. Gymkhana itself, named for the colonial-era sporting clubs later opened to Indian high society, has become shorthand for Indian cooking taken seriously at the highest tier of global dining.

The American push follows a deliberate sequence. Gymkhana opened its first U.S. restaurant at the Aria Resort in Las Vegas in late 2025; the retail line, co-founded with Gulrez Arora, is the natural extension. "This isn't just a product launch," Arora said. "It's the beginning of Indian food's premium moment in America, and Whole Foods is exactly where that story should start."

## Current Developments

The lineup is built from the restaurant's best-selling recipes: butter masala, Goan coconut curry, korma, tikka masala and madras simmer sauces, alongside classic tandoori barbecue, green tikka and roasted garlic-and-chili marinades. Each is engineered to deliver a restaurant-quality plate in under 30 minutes with the addition of a single protein or vegetable. The sauces retail for $8 to $10 — a clear premium over the legacy jarred-curry shelf, and a price point that signals the brand's positioning squarely against the wellness-and-quality crowd that defines the Whole Foods shopper.

Gymkhana is not moving alone. The CPG launch arrives amid a broader wave of investor interest in elevated Indian food. Last year, private-equity firm L Catterton invested in Dishoom, another acclaimed London concept now eyeing American expansion. The pattern is consistent: capital is flowing toward Indian brands that pair credible culinary pedigree with the design and storytelling that premium American grocery demands.

## Diaspora Impact

For the Indian diaspora, the Gymkhana launch is a double-edged delight. On one hand, it validates a cuisine that NRI families have long felt was underestimated in the West — finally, a curry on the Whole Foods shelf that does not apologize for itself. On the other, it raises the eternal diaspora question of authenticity and price: many NRI cooks can make a better butter masala from scratch for a fraction of $10, and may bristle at a London brand selling "premium" Indian flavor to Americans.

Yet the convenience argument is real, especially for second-generation NRIs who grew up on home cooking but lack the time or technique to reproduce it. A jar that genuinely tastes restaurant-grade lowers the barrier to weeknight Indian food and, perhaps more importantly, normalizes regional specificity — Goan coconut, madras heat — for American shoppers accustomed to a flattened "curry."

## What's Next

The wager is that Indian food is following the trajectory of other once-niche cuisines into the premium center of the American grocery store. If Gymkhana's sauces move at Whole Foods, expect the line to broaden — chutneys, dals, ready meals — and competitors to crowd in. The risk is the familiar one for restaurant-to-retail leaps: a Michelin name guarantees attention but not repeat purchase, and the American shelf is littered with chef-branded jars that launched loud and faded fast.

For now, Gymkhana has placed its bet where it believes the story belongs — and the broader signal, of serious money chasing serious Indian food, may matter more than any single jar of korma.
